evidenceAudit.scope: Adults with acute chest pain in the emergency setting: recognition of acute coronary syndrome, early ECG and hs-troponin strategy, first-line treatment, and exclusion of life-threatening non-coronary causes. Verified against NICE CG95, HTG552, NG185 and NG158 and the Saudi Heart Association ACS guideline.
findings: Every threshold, dose and timing in this topic was read from the cited source section on 13 Oct 2026 (NICE CG95, NICE HTG552, NICE NG185, NICE NG158 and the Saudi Heart Association ACS guideline).
The SHA guideline has no printed publication year; page locators are the printed page numbers.
Normal values are typical adult ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: SFDA registration and formulary not checked (SFDA register could not be reached from the authoring environment)
GTN and opioid doses not stated in the cited sources and not reproduced
Aortic dissection and pulmonary embolism presenting features are not listed in the cited sources; only the NICE PE Wells criteria are given
ESC and AHA/ACC chest pain guidelines were not opened

pathophysiology.summary: Acute chest pain is a symptom with cardiac and non-cardiac causes. The aim in the first hour is to identify acute coronary syndrome (ACS) and the other life-threatening causes, and to start treatment without delaying transfer.
keyMechanisms: ACS: thrombus forms on a ruptured atheromatous plaque and partly or fully blocks a coronary artery, injuring myocardium (SHA printed pp. 7 and 22–23).
Stable angina: ischaemic pain that is constricting, brought on by exertion and relieved by rest or GTN within about 5 minutes (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.3.3.1).
Troponin rises and falls after myocardial injury, but a raised value is not specific to ACS: myocarditis, aortic dissection and pulmonary embolism also raise it (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.2.6.2).
Life-threatening non-coronary causes to exclude early: pulmonary embolism, aortic dissection, pneumonia and pneumothorax (NICE CG95 Recs 1.2.2.8 and 1.2.6.8).

references.title: NICE CG95: Recent-onset chest pain of suspected cardiac origin: assessment and diagnosis
references.edition: NICE guideline, updated 30 November 2016, Recommendations 1.2.2.8, 1.2.6.2, 1.2.6.8 and 1.3.3.1

symptoms: Pain in the chest and/or arms, back or jaw lasting longer than 15 minutes (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.2.1.3).
Chest pain with nausea and vomiting, marked sweating or breathlessness, or a combination (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.2.1.3).
New-onset chest pain, or abrupt worsening of stable angina, with frequent episodes on little or no exertion, often lasting longer than 15 minutes (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.2.1.3).
Chest pressure or discomfort lasting at least several minutes, sometimes with sweating, dyspnoea, nausea or anxiety (SHA printed p. 23).
Not every ACS presents with central chest pain; do not score symptoms differently by sex or ethnic group (NICE CG95 Recs 1.2.1.5–1.2.1.6).
physicalSigns: Haemodynamic status: pulse and blood pressure (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.2.4.2; NICE NG185 Rec. 1.2.8).
Signs of ACS complications: pulmonary oedema, cardiogenic shock (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.2.4.2).
Signs of non-coronary causes, for example aortic dissection (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.2.4.2).
redFlags: Chest pain now, or pain within the last 12 hours with an abnormal or unavailable resting ECG: emergency hospital referral (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.2.1.7).
ST elevation or presumed new left bundle branch block on ECG: treat as STEMI (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.2.2.2).
Chest pain with haemodynamic instability (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.2.1.3).

Ongoing ischaemia, haemodynamic compromise, arrhythmia, mechanical complication, acute heart failure or recurrent dynamic ST/T changes: very high risk, immediate invasive strategy within 2 hours (SHA printed p. 24).
Further chest pain after a recent confirmed or suspected ACS: emergency referral (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.2.1.11).
precipitants: Physical exertion: anginal pain is brought on by exertion and relieved by rest or GTN within about 5 minutes (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.3.3.1).
Frequent episodes on little or no exertion suggest an unstable pattern (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.2.1.3).

Risk factors that raise the likelihood of coronary disease: diabetes, smoking, hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia, family history of coronary disease, obesity, known atherosclerosis (SHA printed p. 13; NICE CG95 Rec. 1.3.3.4).

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Pain with all 3 features: constricting discomfort in the chest, neck, shoulders, jaw or arms; brought on by exertion; relieved by rest or GTN within about 5 minutes. Two features = atypical angina; one or none = non-anginal (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.3.3.1).

Score with the two-level PE Wells score (more than 4 points = PE likely): clinical DVT signs, alternative diagnosis less likely than PE, heart rate over 100/min, immobilisation over 3 days or surgery within 4 weeks, previous DVT/PE, haemoptysis, malignancy (NICE NG158 Rec. 1.1.17, Table 2).

Look for it on examination and keep it in mind when troponin is raised; early CT is used to exclude it, not to diagnose ACS (NICE CG95 Recs 1.2.4.2, 1.2.6.2 and 1.2.6.7). Neither source lists distinguishing symptoms.
Chest X-ray helps exclude both (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.2.6.8). Pain brought on by breathing in makes angina unlikely (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.3.3.5).
Causes a raised troponin without ACS; reassess for other causes before confirming ACS when troponin is raised (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.2.6.2).

Pain that is continuous or very prolonged, unrelated to activity, brought on by breathing in, or accompanied by dizziness, palpitations, tingling or difficulty swallowing makes angina unlikely (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.3.3.5).

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Suspected ACS and pain now, or pain-free but pain within 12 hours and ECG abnormal or not available
Pain within 12 hours now resolved with a normal ECG, or last pain 12 to 72 hours ago
As soon as possible at first medical contact; maximum 10 minutes

diagnosticCriteria.criterion: Myocardial infarction (universal definition, NICE CG95 Rec. 1.2.6.1)
diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Rise and/or fall of troponin with at least one value above the 99th percentile, plus ischaemic symptoms, new ST-T change or new LBBB, pathological Q waves, imaging evidence of new loss of viable myocardium or wall motion abnormality, or intracoronary thrombus at angiography
Highly suspicious 2; moderately suspicious 1; slightly or non-suspicious 0
Significant ST depression 2; non-specific repolarisation change 1; normal 0
Over 65 = 2; over 45 to under 65 = 1; under 45 = 0 (as printed; ages exactly 45 and 65 are not assigned)

diagnosticCriteria.criterion: HEART score: Risk factors (SHA printed p. 13)
diagnosticCriteria.threshold: 3 risk factors or known atherosclerotic disease 2; 1 or 2 risk factors 1; none 0
More than 3 times the normal limit 2; more than 1 to under 3 times 1; below the normal limit 0
Score below 3 predicts a 30-day major adverse cardiac event miss rate of 0% to 2%
3 of 3 features = typical; 2 = atypical; 0 or 1 = non-anginal

ruleIn.expectedFinding: Regional ST elevation or presumed new LBBB (STEMI); ST depression or deep T-wave inversion (NSTEMI or unstable angina); Q waves or T-wave change raise suspicion. A normal ECG does not exclude ACS.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Record within 10 minutes of first medical contact and send it ahead; do not delay transfer (SHA printed p. 12; NICE CG95 Rec. 1.2.2.1). If in doubt, repeat the ECG, review old ECGs or add leads (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.2.2.6).
ruleIn.normalValue: Sinus rhythm with no ST-segment or T-wave change, no pathological Q waves, no LBBB

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Venous blood on arrival, then repeat per assay
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Rise and/or fall with at least one value above the 99th percentile; a detectable first value does not by itself confirm MI.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Take on arrival (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.2.4.1). High or moderate risk: serial samples as in HTG552. Low risk: repeat if the first is positive; a single sample below the limit of detection can rule out NSTEMI (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.2.5.3; HTG552 Rec. 1.2). Interpret with time from onset, ECG, pre-test probability and chronic elevation (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.2.5.7).
ruleIn.normalValue: Below the assay limit of detection and the 99th percentile (assay- and sex-specific; local laboratory ranges apply)

ruleIn.targetCondition: Hypoxaemia in ACS or other causes
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Do not give oxygen routinely. Give oxygen only if SpO2 is below 94% (target 94–98%), or 88–92% in COPD at risk of hypercapnic failure until blood gases are available (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.2.3.3). Some oximeters misread, especially with dark skin.
ruleIn.normalValue: 94% or above (the threshold below which NICE advises oxygen)

ruleIn.targetCondition: Complications of ACS or alternative diagnoses
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Pulmonary oedema (complication of ACS), pneumothorax or consolidation.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Consider it to exclude ACS complications or other diagnoses such as pneumothorax and pneumonia (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.2.6.8). If PE is suspected, also offer it to exclude other causes (NICE NG158 Rec. 1.1.15).
ruleIn.normalValue: Normal heart size and lung fields; no oedema, pneumothorax or consolidation

ruleOut.testName: CT pulmonary angiogram or CT of the aorta
ruleOut.modalityTarget: CT, only when PE or aortic dissection is suspected
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Pulmonary artery filling defect (PE) or aortic dissection.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Use early chest CT to rule out other diagnoses such as PE or aortic dissection, not to diagnose ACS (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.2.6.7). If PE is likely (Wells over 4 points), offer CTPA immediately if possible (NICE NG158 Rec. 1.1.18).
ruleOut.normalValue: No pulmonary artery filling defect and no aortic dissection

ruleOut.modalityTarget: Venous blood or point-of-care quantitative test
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Above the assay threshold: proceed to CTPA.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: PE Wells score of 4 or less: D-dimer with the result within 4 hours if possible; if not available in 4 hours, give interim anticoagulation while waiting. Negative D-dimer: stop interim anticoagulation and think of other diagnoses (NICE NG158 Rec. 1.1.21). Consider an age-adjusted threshold over 50 years (NICE NG158 Rec. 1.1.14).
ruleOut.normalValue: Below the assay threshold (an age-adjusted threshold may be used over 50 years)

clinicalManagement.title: First medical contact
actions: Ask if pain is present now. If pain-free, ask when the last episode was, especially within the last 12 hours (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.2.1.1).
Record a 12-lead ECG at first medical contact, target within 10 minutes. Send it ahead and do not delay transfer (SHA printed p. 12; NICE CG95 Rec. 1.2.2.1).

Aspirin single loading dose unless clear allergy: 300 mg (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.2.3.2); the Saudi Heart Association gives 150–300 mg orally (SHA printed p. 11). See the comparison table. Give no other antiplatelet before hospital (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.2.3.2).

Pain relief: GTN sublingual or buccal, or IV opioid such as morphine especially if MI is suspected (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.2.3.1). SHA advises against routine IV opioid for STEMI-related discomfort, with selective use for severe pain (SHA printed p. 11).

Oxygen only if SpO2 is below 94% (target 94–98%; 88–92% in COPD at risk of hypercapnic failure) (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.2.3.3). SHA advises avoiding routine oxygen in STEMI with SpO2 of 90% or more (SHA printed p. 11).

Do not use the response to GTN as a diagnostic test (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.2.1.4). Do not offer dual antiplatelet therapy to people with chest pain before a diagnosis of unstable angina or NSTEMI (NICE NG185 Rec. 1.2.6).
Monitor pain, pulse and blood pressure, rhythm, SpO2 and repeat ECGs, and check pain relief, until a firm diagnosis is made (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.2.3.4).

clinicalManagement.title: Triage by ECG
actions: Choose the pathway from the first ECG; a normal ECG does not exclude ACS (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.2.2.5).

branches.condition: ST elevation or presumed new LBBB (STEMI)
actions: Assess immediately for reperfusion, primary PCI or fibrinolysis, and deliver it as quickly as possible (NICE NG185 Recs 1.1.1 and 1.1.3).

Target first-medical-contact-to-device time of 90 minutes or less at a PCI-capable centre and 120 minutes or less including transfer; consider fibrinolysis if this cannot be met (SHA printed pp. 15–16).
Transfer patients with a suspected STEMI directly to a PCI-capable centre and, if PCI is planned, straight to the catheter laboratory (SHA printed pp. 11–12).

branches.condition: ST depression or deep T-wave inversion
actions: Manage as NSTEMI or unstable angina using NICE NG185 section 1.2 and the Non-ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction topic (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.2.2.3).

branches.condition: Other ECG change (Q waves, T-wave change) or non-diagnostic ECG
actions: Keep a high index of suspicion for ACS with Q waves or T-wave change (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.2.2.4).
Repeat serial ECGs and run the troponin pathway below (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.2.2.6).

branches.condition: Last pain more than 72 hours ago and no complications
actions: Do a detailed clinical assessment, resting 12-lead ECG and troponin, interpreting troponin against the time since the event (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.2.1.10).

clinicalManagement.title: Troponin and risk stratification
clinicalManagement.timeframe: On arrival; repeat at 30 minutes to 3 hours depending on assay
actions: Take high-sensitivity troponin on arrival (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.2.4.1). High or moderate risk: serial samples. Low risk: repeat if the first is positive; consider one sample at presentation only if it is below the limit of detection (NICE CG95 Recs 1.2.5.2–1.2.5.3).

Early rule-out options are a single sample on presentation at or near the limit of detection, or a second sample 30 minutes to 3 hours after the first; use clinical judgement and the likely time from symptom onset (HTG552 Rec. 1.2).
Use the HEART score to risk-stratify suspected ACS without ST elevation; a score below 3 predicts a 30-day MACE miss rate of 0% to 2% (SHA printed p. 12).
Diagnose MI with the universal definition. If troponin is raised, reassess for myocarditis, aortic dissection and PE before confirming ACS (NICE CG95 Recs 1.2.6.1–1.2.6.2).
Do not use natriuretic peptides or hs-CRP to diagnose ACS (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.2.5.5). Do not routinely offer non-invasive imaging or exercise ECG in the initial assessment (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.2.6.6).

clinicalManagement.title: If ACS is unlikely or excluded
actions: Consider life-threatening alternatives first: PE, aortic dissection, pneumonia (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.2.2.8). Add a chest X-ray for pneumothorax, pneumonia or pulmonary oedema (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.2.6.8).
Suspected PE: PE Wells score. More than 4 points: CTPA immediately if possible, otherwise interim anticoagulation. 4 points or fewer: D-dimer within 4 hours (NICE NG158 Recs 1.1.17–1.1.21).
No troponin rise and no acute ECG change: reassess whether the pain is cardiac. If ischaemia is still suspected, follow the stable chest pain steps (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.2.6.5).

Stable chest pain: 64-slice (or above) CT coronary angiography for typical or atypical angina, or non-anginal pain with ST-T change or Q waves on ECG (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.3.4.3). Offer functional imaging if CT shows disease of uncertain significance (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.3.5.1); invasive angiography is third line (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.3.5.2).
If ACS is excluded but cardiovascular risk factors are present, follow the cardiovascular risk and hypertension guidance (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.2.6.9).

clinicalManagement.title: Escalation and disposition
actions: STEMI: activate the catheter laboratory (SHA printed pp. 15–16). Very high-risk NSTE-ACS features: immediate invasive strategy within 2 hours of admission (SHA printed p. 24).
NSTE-ACS: admit to a monitored unit with continuous rhythm monitoring for at least 24 hours or until the diagnosis is ruled out (SHA printed p. 26).

Rule-out: people whose troponin stays below the early rule-out threshold may not need admission (HTG552, rationale). Same-day assessment applies if pain was within 12 hours but is now resolved with a normal ECG, or the last pain was 12 to 72 hours ago (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.2.1.8).
Explain if the pain is non-cardiac and refer for further investigation if appropriate. Give individual advice on seeking help if pain recurs (NICE CG95 Recs 1.1.1.8–1.1.1.9).

regimens.dose: Loading dose: 300 mg (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.2.3.2); the Saudi Heart Association gives 150–300 mg (SHA printed p. 11)
regimens.duration: Single dose before diagnosis; ongoing aspirin follows the ACS pathway if ACS is confirmed
adjustments: No dose adjustment for the single loading dose is stated in NICE CG95 or the SHA guideline
Do not give if there is clear evidence of aspirin allergy (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.2.3.2)
monitoring: Pulse, blood pressure, rhythm, SpO2 and pain relief until a firm diagnosis (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.2.3.4)
If given before arrival, send a written record with the patient (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.2.3.2)
contraindications: Clear evidence of aspirin allergy (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.2.3.2)

medicationPlan.note: Only the aspirin loading dose is given as a dose in NICE CG95 and the SHA guideline. GTN and opioid doses are not stated in either source, so follow product information. Check SFDA registration and the hospital formulary.

learningObjectives: Recognise the presentations that need emergency referral and record an ECG within 10 minutes.
Use hs-troponin early rule-out strategies and the HEART score appropriately, and know their limits.
Exclude life-threatening non-coronary causes of chest pain: PE, aortic dissection, pneumonia and pneumothorax.
keyPoints: ECG within 10 minutes of first medical contact; a normal ECG does not exclude ACS.
Aspirin loading dose 300 mg (NICE) or 150–300 mg (SHA) unless clear allergy.
Oxygen only if SpO2 is below 94% (NICE); avoid routine oxygen in STEMI with SpO2 of 90% or more (SHA).
A single hs-troponin below the limit of detection at presentation can rule out NSTEMI in low-risk patients; a detectable value alone does not confirm MI.
pitfalls: Using the response to GTN to make the diagnosis (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.2.1.4).
Scoring symptoms differently in women or by ethnic group (NICE CG95 Recs 1.2.1.5–1.2.1.6).
Giving dual antiplatelet therapy before a diagnosis of unstable angina or NSTEMI is made (NICE NG185 Rec. 1.2.6).
Treating any troponin rise as ACS without considering myocarditis, aortic dissection or PE (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.2.6.2).
Using early CT to diagnose ACS; it is for excluding other diagnoses (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.2.6.7).

patientEducation: Explain the possible causes of the symptoms and the uncertainty, and correct misinformation (NICE CG95 Recs 1.1.1.1–1.1.1.2).
Explain each test, its purpose, limits and risks, including radiation, in plain language (NICE CG95 Recs 1.1.1.4–1.1.1.5).
Explain that a detectable troponin on the first test does not necessarily mean a heart attack (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.2.5.4).
Give individual advice on when to seek help if chest pain returns (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.1.1.9).
lifestyleAndDiet: If ACS is excluded but cardiovascular risk factors are present, follow the cardiovascular disease and hypertension guidance (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.2.6.9).
Identify smokers and give repeated advice to stop, with follow-up support and nicotine replacement, varenicline or bupropion (SHA printed p. 26).
mdtReferrals: Cardiology for confirmed or suspected ACS and for revascularisation decisions (NICE NG185 Rec. 1.2.25).
Further investigation or referral if the pain is non-cardiac and the cause is unknown (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.1.1.8).
dischargeCriteria: No diagnostic ECG change, hs-troponin below the early rule-out threshold for the assay, and life-threatening alternatives considered (HTG552 Rec. 1.2; NICE CG95 Rec. 1.2.2.8).
Cause explained, or onward referral arranged, and advice on seeking help given (NICE CG95 Recs 1.1.1.8–1.1.1.9).
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Arrange same-day assessment if pain was within 12 hours but is resolved with a normal ECG, or the last pain was 12 to 72 hours ago (NICE CG95 Rec. 1.2.1.8). For suspected stable angina, arrange CT coronary angiography or functional testing as in NICE CG95 Recs 1.3.4.3–1.3.5.2.
